'''''Adiantum capillus-veneris''''', the '''maidenhair fern''',<ref name="PlantAtlas">{{cite web | title=Maidenhair Fern ''Adiantum capillus-veneris'' L. | website=PlantAtlas | url=https://plantatlas2020.org/atlas/2cd4p9h.x63 | access-date=2025-09-30}}</ref><ref name=BSBI07>{{BSBI 2007 |access-date=2014-10-17 }}</ref> '''southern maidenhair fern''', '''black maidenhair fern''' and '''venus hair fern''', is a species of [[fern]]s in the genus ''[[Adiantum]]'' and the family [[Pteridaceae]]<ref name="Christenhusz-2011"/> with a subcosmopolitan worldwide distribution. It is cultivated as a popular [[ornamental plant|garden fern]] and [[houseplant]].<ref name="wild">[http://www.wildflower.org/plants/result.php?id_plant=ADCA Wildflower.org-NPIN: Adiantum capillus-veneris (Southern maidenhair fern)]. accessed 4.04.2011</ref>

==Distribution==
''Adiantum capillus-veneris'' is native to humid warm temperate to tropical regions globally. It occurs in western and southern [[Europe]] (north to southern [[Scotland]], where its northernmost sites are found<ref name="PlantAtlas"/>), much of [[Africa]], the [[Levant]] and across [[Asia]] to [[Japan]], in [[Australasia]], and in the Americas in the southern half of the United States from [[California]] to the Atlantic coast, through Mexico and Central America, to South America.<ref name="POWO">{{cite web | title=''Adiantum capillus-veneris'' L. | website=Plants of the World Online | date=2018-07-03 | url=https://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:325030-2 | access-date=2025-09-30}}</ref><ref name="wild"/><ref>[http://scitec.uwichill.edu.bb/bcs/staff/lec/Fern_species/adiantum_capillus-veneris.htm  The University of the West Indies, Cave Hill]{{Dead link|date=October 2025 |bot=InternetArchiveBot }}</ref><ref name="cundall">Cundall. P., (2004) Native Plants: The definitive guide to Australian plants, Global Book Publishing Lane Cove, N.S.W, p.298, {{ISBN|978-1-74048-027-7}}</ref> There are two disjunct occurrences in the northern part of North America, at Cascade Springs in the [[Black Hills]] of [[South Dakota]] and [[Fairmont Hot Springs, British Columbia]]. In both instances, the warm microclimate created by hot mineral springs permits the growth of the plant far north of its normal range. It is similar in Zvonce spa resort (Звоначка Бања, Zvonačka Banja), near Pirot in Serbia, where hot mineral springs provide adequate heat and humidity for the survival of this species.<ref>{{cite web|website=Pirotske Vesti|url=http://www.pirotskevesti.rs/babusnica/zasticeno-jedino-staniste-venerine-vlasi-u-srbiji/|title=Zaštićeno jedino stanište venerine vlasi u Srbiji|date=11 December 2015|language=serbian|trans-title=The Only Habitat of the Venus Hair Fern in Serbia is Now Protected}}</ref>

It is found in temperate climates from warm-temperate to tropical, where the moisture content is high but not saturated, in the moist, well-drained sand, loam or limestone of many [[habitat]]s, including rainforests, shrub and woodlands, broadleaf and coniferous forests, and desert cliff [[Seep (hydrology)|seep]]s, and [[Spring (hydrosphere)|spring]]s. It often may be seen growing on moist, sheltered and shaded [[sandstone]] or [[limestone]] formations, generally south-facing in the southern hemisphere, north-facing in the north, or in gorges.<ref name="wild"/> It occurs throughout Africa in moist places by streams.<ref name="SimTR">{{cite book | last = Sim | first = Thomas Robertson |author-link=Thomas Robertson Sim | title = The Ferns of South Africa| url = https://archive.org/details/fernsofsouthafri00simt | publisher = Cambridge University Press | location = London & Edinburgh | year = 1915 }}</ref> On moist sandstone cliffs it grows in full or partial shade, even when unprotected.<ref name="RouxJP">{{cite book | last = Roux | first = J.P. | title = Cape Peninsula Ferns | publisher = National Botanic Gardens of South Africa | location = Kirstenbosch | year = 1979 | isbn = 978-0-620-03775-4 }}</ref>

Botanists were surprised to find it thriving in the 14th-century underground tunnels of [[Znojmo]], [[South Moravian Region|South Moravia]]. The fern was first found in the tunnels in 2020 and has since spread significantly, thanks to the damp environment and artificial lighting from tourist tours. One theory suggests the fern's spores originated from a houseplant in Znojmo, while another proposes they traveled from a tropical country. Despite its unusual location, the fern is not expected to spread beyond the tunnels or harm local species.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2025-03-14 |title=Botanists stunned by tropical fern flourishing in Znojmo's underground tunnels |url=https://english.radio.cz/botanists-stunned-tropical-fern-flourishing-znojmos-underground-tunnels-8845581 |access-date=2025-03-24 |website=Radio Prague International |language=en}}</ref>

==Description==
''Adiantum capillus-veneris'' grows from {{convert|15|to|30|cm|in|0|abbr=on}} in height; its fronds arising in clusters from creeping rhizomes {{convert|20|to|70|cm|in|0|abbr=on}} tall, with very delicate, light green [[frond]]s much subdivided into pinnae {{convert|5|to|10|mm|in|1|abbr=on}} long and broad; the frond rachis is black and wiry.<ref name="wild"/><ref name="cundall"/>

==Cultivation==
''Adiantum capillus-veneris''  is cultivated and widely available around the world for planting in [[Natural landscaping|natural landscape]] [[native plant]]s and traditional [[shade garden]]s, for outdoor [[container garden]]s, and commonly as an indoor [[houseplant]].

''[[Adiantum × mairisii]]'' is a winter hardy hybrid of ''Adiantum capillus-veneris'' with another species, which is likely to be one of ''Adiantum raddianum'', ''Adiantum aethiopicum'', or ''Adiantum cuneatum''.<ref name=":1">{{Cite web|title=Pacific Horticulture {{!}} Pacific Plant Promotions: Adiantum xmairisii|url=https://www.pacifichorticulture.org/articles/pacific-plant-promotions-adiantum-mairisii/|access-date=2021-07-21|website=Pacific Horticulture|language=en}}</ref>

As a houseplant, ''Adiantum capillus-veneris''  requires filtered light and very humid conditions. It should be grown in soil rich in organic matter and should be watered frequently but lightly, to keep the roots damp but not drenched. The temperature should not fall below {{convert|12|C|}}. It is propagated by dividing, making sure each clump has a section of rhizome.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Chiusoli |first1=Alessandro |last2=Boriani |first2=Luisa Maria |title=Simon & Schuster's guide to houseplants |date=1986 |publisher=Simon and Schuster |location=New York |isbn=0-671-63131-4}}</ref>

==Conservation==
The fern is listed as an [[endangered species]] in [[North Carolina]] (as southern maidenhair-fern) and [[threatened species]] in [[Kentucky]] (as venus hair fern), due to loss of [[Appalachia]]n habitat.

==Traditional uses==
This plant is used medicinally by Native Americans. The [[Mahuna people]] use the plant internally for rheumatism,<ref>Romero, John Bruno 1954 The Botanical Lore of the California Indians. New York. Vantage Press, Inc. (p. 60)</ref> and the [[Navajo people]] of [[Kayenta, Arizona]] use an [[infusion]] of the plant as a lotion for bumblebee and centipede stings.<ref name="Wyman, Leland C p. 14">Wyman, Leland C. and Stuart K. Harris 1951 The Ethnobotany of the Kayenta Navaho. Albuquerque. The University of New Mexico Press (p. 14)</ref> The Navajo people also smoke it or take it internally to treat mental illness.<ref name="Wyman, Leland C p. 14"/>

In the traditional medicine of Iran, frond infusion of ''Adiantum capillus-veneris'' is used for [[jaundice]] therapy.<ref>{{Cite journal |doi = 10.3389/fphar.2017.00518|pmid = 28860989|pmc = 5559545|title = Ethnopharmacological Approaches for Therapy of Jaundice: Part I|year = 2017|last1 = Tewari|first1 = Devesh|last2 = Mocan|first2 = Andrei|last3 = Parvanov|first3 = Emil D.|last4 = Sah|first4 = Archana N.|last5 = Nabavi|first5 = Seyed M.|last6 = Huminiecki|first6 = Lukasz|last7 = Ma|first7 = Zheng Feei|last8 = Lee|first8 = Yeong Yeh|last9 = Horbańczuk|first9 = Jarosław O.|last10 = Atanasov|first10 = Atanas G.|journal = Frontiers in Pharmacology|volume = 8|article-number = 518|doi-access = free}}</ref> Along with this, they have a wide range of medicinal uses and have been used to treat coughs, cold, and to aid in kidney function.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Al Snafi |first1=Ali |title=The Chemical Constituents and Pharmacological Effects of ''Adiantum Capillus-Veneris'' |journal=Asian Journal of Pharmaceutical Science & Technology |date=2015 |volume=5 |issue=2 |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/297700715}}</ref>
